abstractText:
Modern software is complex and continuously evolving. For every small change to the code, there is a risk of introducing unintended consequences that can affect the software's correctness, security, and performance. To guard against such issues, known as regression bugs, developers must test their software on a diverse suite of program inputs after every code change. However, manually hand-crafting such test inputs risks missing out on important corner cases. This research is developing techniques for automatically generating test inputs that guard against future regressions. The research will focus on automatically synthesizing test inputs that are easy to maintain, quick to execute, and robust at detecting faults introduced by small code changes. The technology developed in this project is intended to help improve the reliability of critical software systems, cut down energy usage during development, and reduce technical debt. Furthermore, this research is also contributing to the investigator's ongoing efforts in developing reusable course material for undergraduate computer science education, in particular, by incorporating the automatic test-input generation technology in classroom programming assignments. The project activities themselves will also provide research experience opportunities for a diverse cohort of undergraduate students.

Randomized test-input generation techniques such as grey-box fuzzing have been successful at uncovering critical bugs and security issues in widely used software. However, conventional fuzz testing requires generating billions of test inputs using hundreds of CPU-hours in order to be effective, which is impractical for continuously validating code changes. This project shifts the focus of fuzz-testing research towards generating a reusable corpus of regression test inputs, in order to support software evolution. The research is focusing on optimizing the quality of the generated test inputs along three dimensions. First, an iterative ensemble fuzzing technique is being developed for synthesizing test inputs that are concise by construction. Second, mutation analysis is being used to guide fuzzing towards synthesizing test inputs that are robust at detecting faults due to small code changes. Third, language modeling techniques are being used to learn common patterns in human-authored test inputs. The models are being used to develop novel fuzzing algorithms that can synthesize natural-looking test inputs that easier to maintain as the software evolves.  The results of this research are being disseminated in the form of open-source tools and publications that are intended to help software developers reduce maintenance costs and ultimately deploy more reliable software.

projectOutComesReport:
ur society depends critically on complex software systems which are continuously adapting as technology and market conditions evolve. For every small change to the code, there is a risk of introducing unintended consequences that can affect the software's correctness, security, and performance. To guard against such issues, known as regressions, engineers must test their software on a diverse suite of program inputs after every code change. This project investigated techniques for automatically generating high-quality test inputs that guard against future regressions. 


A significant focus of the project was on improving the technology behind fuzz testing, a popular approach for automating test-input generation via algorithms that use randomness to quickly search through the vast space of all possible inputs. This project improved upon the state-of-the-art of fuzz testing by developing a new technique that focuses the random search on the ability to generate test inputs that are likely to detect program faults. This is done using the concept of "mutation testing", where a program is modified to inject artificial faults, and test inputs are evaluated by whether executing the original and mutated program on the inputs causes a measurable difference in behavior. In this project, the researchers implemented a fuzz testing technique for Java programs that takes into account mutation-distinguishing ability. An empirical evaluation on widely used open-source software indicated that this approach indeed improves the robustness of generated inputs towards future faults, such as regression bugs. This enhanced fuzz testing tool, called "Mu2" has been made open-source for the public to use or extend. 


The project further investigated how fuzz testing generates new inputs for programs that process highly structured input data, such as database queries or XML documents. A key part of the fuzz testing algorithm is performing random mutations on previously generated inputs in order to synthesize new inputs, much like genetic mutations in cell biology. The researchers identified that prior techniques for performing mutations completely randomly could lead to disruptions in the structural integrity of generated test inputs, such as queries, rendering them meaningless and thereby wasting computational resources during fuzz testing. The researchers studied this phenomenon, calling it the "Havoc Effect", by empirically evaluating variants of fuzz testing algorithms on widely used open-source Java software. The researchers also prototyped new techniques that can mitigate this effect using program execution monitoring to identify how random mutations affect various parts of the input structure. The experimental results indicated that while the havoc effect can be mitigated, in practice this does not significantly affect the success of fuzz testing for most programs that read inputs in sequence, which is very common.


The project also studied the statistical properties of test inputs synthesized by fuzz testing tools by comparing them to test inputs written by humans, using techniques of language modeling from the field of machine learning. An empirical analysis on fuzz testing tools for compilers, whose inputs are C programs, provided surprising results that automatically generated inputs are more statistically repetitive than human written programs as extracted from open-source software repositories. This finding has future implications for fuzz testing research, as it indicates that language models could be used to control and selectively maximize the amount of random surprising information in order to uncover edge-case software bugs.

Finally, the project investigated other directions relating software fuzz testing and regression bugs, such as (i) using modern large language models (LLMs) to automatically synthesize the skeleton code required to enable fuzz testing in the first place, (ii) identifying, via an empirical analysis on open-source software, that many edge-case regression bugs arise due to mishandling of date and time computations dealing with timezones or daylight savings, and (iii) identifying, via a survey of prior work, that the state-of-the-practice in automatic testing is inadequate for programs that make use of concurrent multi-threading for performing multiple tasks in parallel in the same program. 


All of the research conducted in this project has been made available via open-access publications and/or open source software artifacts. The techniques developed in this project have been referenced in subsequent studies by other researchers, and are being adopted by practitioners in industry. These results will positively impact the reliability and security of critical software systems that our society relies on.

abstractText:
Software performance is critical for most software systems to achieve scale and limit operating costs and energy consumption. As modern software systems, such as big data and machine-learning systems, are increasingly built by composing many reusable infrastructure components and deployed on distributed and heterogeneous hardware, developers have powerful tools and abstractions at their fingertips, and as a result face immense configuration complexity. Software and hardware need to be selected and configured carefully to achieve high performance for a given system and task. Unfortunately, in practice, performance faults and misconfigurations are common, where a system performs much worse than expected, not achieving its mission or simply wasting cost and energy. In large configuration spaces, end-users and developers face severe challenges in understanding and fixing performance faults by changing software configuration, changing hardware deployment, or modifying the software's code itself. Current approaches that model system performance by analyzing correlations among performance measurements and options are slow and may produce misleading results, obfuscating the actual causes of performance faults. Even if they can fix the problem, most of them cannot explain why (1) the obtained configurations are the real cause of the problem, and (2) a user/developer should consider the proposed recommendations. In both cases, the lack of explainability is a big issue. The project is intended to initiate a paradigm shift in today's testing and debugging methodology for complex, highly configurable systems, thereby positively impacting a broad range of industrial sectors relying on complex, highly configurable systems. Specifically, the project contributes to substantial energy savings and reduced carbon emissions, especially for the many big-data and machine-learning systems that operate at a massive scale. Finally, the research is providing valuable training for involved students from diverse backgrounds in research and generating high-quality researchers and practitioners for society.
 
This project develops and evaluates foundations and tools for a causal approach to performance modeling and performance debugging. This project introduces the new concept of causal performance models that are learned using causal structure learning by intervening over configuration options and observing system performance regarding (multiple) performance objectives, rather than just analyzing correlations. Causal models enable causal inference and counterfactual reasoning for numerous tasks, including debugging performance faults and misconfigurations. Based on a solid technical foundation of causal modeling and extensive experience with performance modeling for configurable systems, this project develops innovations in three thrusts: (1) It designs and refines a causal modeling approach for software performance of systems composed of multiple configurable components, using innovations in sampling strategies, code analysis, compositional reasoning, and transfer learning to build accurate causal models efficiently. (2) It develops and evaluates user-facing tool support, based on causal models, to help users select well-performing configurations for their specific tasks and hardware and resolve misconfiguration faults with configuration changes, highlighting the (causal) performance impact of configuration decisions and providing a Pareto analysis of involved tradeoffs. (3) It develops and evaluates developer-facing tool support to foster code-level debugging and documentation. Finally, all contributions are being evaluated end-to-end with developers on real performance faults, showing how both users and developers benefit from causal models and related tools.

projectOutComesReport:
This project aimed to make highly configurable computer systems—from cloud software platforms to robots and machine‑learning pipelines—more diagnosable, explainable, and optimizable. Traditional performance tools often rely on correlations that can be misleading, especially when systems evolve or operate under changing environments and workloads. We pioneered a causal performance approach that learns why performance issues occur, not just what correlates with them, enabling more reliable debugging and optimization under real‑world conditions. A core outcome of this work was Unicorn, a causal performance modeling framework that generalized across environments where prior methods failed and outperformed state‑of‑the‑art techniques in identifying performance faults and near‑optimal configurations.

Building on Unicorn's causal modeling foundation, we developed a suite of tools that deliver practical performance gains in real systems. CAMEO leverages causal transfer learning to reduce the configuration search space, accelerating optimization across environments. In machine‑learning inference pipelines, IPA dynamically reconfigures resources and model variants to balance latency, cost, and accuracy, achieving up to 21% improvement in accuracy with minimal cost increase over standard approaches. Related work on InfAdapter reduced latency violations by 65% and operational costs by 33% compared to popular autoscalers. For deep learning services more broadly, SelfXit, an unsupervised early‑exit mechanism, reduced computational complexity by up to 58% and improved inference latency by up to 46%, with little to no loss in accuracy.

In systems with physical components, we addressed the combinatorial explosion of configuration options in robotics. CaRE identifies root causes of functional faults through causal analysis and validated these diagnoses across both simulated and physical robots. CuRE (Causal Understanding and Remediation for Enhancing robot performance) further uses causal structure to constrain the optimization search space, enabling faster and more efficient tuning from simulation to real‑world robotic deployments. In addition, FlexiBO introduced a cost‑aware multi‑objective optimization strategy for deep neural networks, producing better Pareto‑optimal solutions with up to 12% lower error under the same evaluation budget. The latest advancement, RESCUE (Robust Exploration with Structural Causal priors for Uncertainty‑aware Efficient optimization), extends these ideas to multi‑objective, multi‑fidelity Bayesian optimization. By guiding exploration with learned causal structure, RESCUE achieved up to a 25% improvement in optimization efficiency on tasks such as robotic grasping and neural architecture tuning, while maintaining robustness in noisy and complex environments.

Complementing these practical tools, the project also advanced foundational understanding of modular performance modeling. Recent work introduced a formal analytical framework that characterizes the inherent difficulty of building performance‑influence models and shows how structural knowledge about a system's modular decomposition can improve modeling effectiveness. This analysis demonstrated that systems with many interacting modules are fundamentally harder to model, but that leveraging structural insights significantly improves both debugging accuracy and performance prediction, helping designers choose appropriate modeling strategies based on system characteristics.

Across all these contributions, the project's causal methodology produced actionable performance insights while fostering open‑source tooling, integration into graduate and undergraduate curricula, and collaborations with industry and government partners. These outcomes demonstrate strong intellectual merit in advancing causal performance understanding and broad impact by reducing engineering effort, improving system reliability, and enabling more sustainable and efficient computing infrastructures.

abstractText:
As society is becoming more and more dependent on software systems, questions arise about how such software can be developed responsibly. In the design of software systems, flexibility and innovation must be balanced with safeguarding the public. Regulators who design policy to steward software’s effect on society often have a hard time capturing clear guidance to hold software systems accountable and keeping up with new technologies, such as the increased use of artificial intelligence (AI). Software engineers have often been left with vague guidance and no measurable goals, such as the EU’s “right to explanation.” While clarifying guidance or court decisions may eventually provide more actionable details, policy implementation is a slow, reactive process that can delay adoption of improvements. To reconcile software and policy design and construct a proactive policy framework for accountable software systems, guidance for qualities such as explainability, safety, and fairness requires more attention.

This project will investigate cross-domain principles for policy design, setting corresponding obligations for software engineers, particularly in the context of AI-supported systems. Results will help stakeholders to deliberately design policy with evidence-based guidance for a specific domain. The project will facilitate interactions between policy makers and software engineers in understanding capabilities and societal expectations toward forming policy goals, investigate policy dimensions and the concrete tradeoffs involved, and connect the policy to specific quality-assurance obligations that could be used in a regulatory evaluation covering both AI and non-AI parts of the system. Specifically, the project will first investigate the important dimensions for policy design (e.g., strictness of regulation, level of evidence, policy specificity) using stakeholder interviews, historical analysis, and technical analysis. It then will evaluate, with several experiments, how design decisions affect outcomes, interact with each other, and result in tradeoffs -- which will be encoded and validated as policy design patterns. The research will combine multiple research methods, including interviews, literature and document analyses, controlled experiments, prototyping, and writer’s workshops. It will deeply integrate social-science research on policy design and regulation with software-engineering research on system design and quality assurance. The research will be disseminated broadly across multiple communities and through engagement with regulators. Educational material will be developed for multiple courses and shared publicly.

projectOutComesReport:
Modern AI-enabled systems are increasingly governed not only by technical performance requirements but also by policy expectations around accountability, transparency, and explainability. Yet policy statements are often either too abstract to guide engineering practice or too prescriptive to remain valid as technology changes. This project investigated cross-domain principles for policy design, drawing on cases in cancer imaging, educational games, and consumer recommender applications. Our goal was to understand how different stakeholders interpret societal expectations and to develop policy design mechanisms for accountability that (1) set future-proof goals, (2) provide practical guidance for regulators and software engineers, and (3) remain flexible enough to evolve. A central theme was connecting policy goals to concrete quality assurance obligations and evidence that can be evaluated in regulatory or organizational review—covering both AI components and the surrounding non-AI software and processes. The overall goal is to improve accountability for software projects through shaping their engineering practices.


Intellectual merit. The project produced multiple complementary research contributions. We analyzed the outcomes of a policy design experiment (initiated via an REU project) and identified nine empirical observations and three recommendations for how to run effective policy design projects. A key insight is that sustained interdisciplinary engagement—rather than one-off consultations—can produce higher-quality, implementable policies, and that this model can be scaled when less-experienced practitioners are guided by experts and supported through research programs. Subsequently, we conducted four iterations of a controlled experiment with over 300 participants examining how developers respond to policy requirements for explanations in the context of an AI-powered medical device (namely, a screening tool for diabetic retinopathy). Unlike many short studies, participants engaged for roughly eight hours each, enabling deeper measurement of how policy framing affects the global and local explanations developers design, the harms they identify, and the tradeoffs they make. In a nutshell, we found that developers without dedicated training struggle to interpret policy and conceptualize evidence; they largely write explanations in an intuitive fashion, ignoring specific policy requirements and user needs. We show that better tooling and educational interventions can help to shape developer actions more effectively when combined with policy. Third, we generated a conceptual bridge between machine-learning explainability and the regulated practice of informed consent in medicine—two contexts that require communicating complex concepts under strong knowledge asymmetry—deriving design lessons and cautions from decades of practice and critique. Finally, we addressed a practical barrier to accountability work: many practitioners view responsible AI processes as irrelevant or bureaucratic. We developed LLM-based tooling to generate short, context-relevant “sticky stories” about ML harms and showed in a controlled experiment that these narratives broaden harm identification and deepen reflection, complementing explainability and accountability efforts.


Broader impacts. The project's broader impacts include explicit suggestions for policy makers, regulators, and engineering teams to align on realistic accountability expectations and on what evidence is needed to evaluate AI-enabled products in practice. We disseminated results through peer-reviewed publications (including ICSE, FAccT, AIES, CHI) and widely used public course materials, and we actively engaged communities beyond our home disciplines. Findings were presented at venues spanning computer science and social science, including FAccT, ICSE, the Eastern Sociological Society meeting, the Society for the Social Studies of Science, and the American Sociological Association. We also delivered invited talks and keynotes to reach cross-disciplinary and practitioner audiences: a keynote at CAIN 2024 (AI Engineering), invited talks at the Symposium on Model Accountability, Sustainability and Healthcare (SMASH) 2025, the Yale School of Medicine, Smith College, and Columbia University's Sociology of Algorithms group, as well as presentations to organizations and practitioner communities such as the Poorvu Center for Teaching and Learning and GE Healthcare. The project trained graduate students, undergraduate research assistants, and multiple REU students in qualitative methods, controlled experimentation, policy analysis, and communication of findings to the public. It also shaped education for large cohorts of future engineers through integration into technical and sociological courses, influenced instruction at multiple universities via openly shared materials, and contributed to new interdisciplinary curricula and textbook development efforts.

abstractText:
This NSF S&CC planning grant contributes to the design and development of new mobility technologies that serve city residents. New mobility technologies are on the rise in cities across the US, with micromobility platforms and autonomous delivery robots occupying the sidewalks of many cities. Amid the enthusiasm around what these devices could mean for the future of transportation and the circulation of essential goods, are concerns about who stands to benefit from these technologies. This research focuses on producing a robust understanding of the unintended harms these devices may introduce and, in collaboration with community members, offer a set of potential opportunities to support resident safety and ensure broad community benefit

Pennsylvania recently passed state-wide legislation classifying personal delivery devices (PDDs) as "pedestrians," bestowing them the same legal rights as human residents. In response, Pittsburgh government officials and residents have come together as a coalition with the aim of developing municipal standards on current delivery devices to ensure continued accessibility of public space, and strategies for planning proactively for future new mobility deployments in the area. Researchers in this project have partnered with the City of Pittsburgh’s Department of Mobility and Infrastructure (DOMI) and established connections with local advocacy organizations to develop community-driven approaches to the deployment and governance of new mobility technologies. Extending methods of impact analysis and equity measures, they draw insights from the actions and perspectives of government officials and residents who are negotiating the changing shape of the city and seeking to define community-driven technology deployments. This planning grant lays the groundwork for a longer-term research with their Pittsburgh partners and other cities, by developing methods and technologies for supporting democratic processes around public PDD deployments.

projectOutComesReport:
New mobility technologies such as sidewalk delivery robots are being developed and deployed in an effort to help improve freight efficiency and reduce carbon emissions, while meeting people’s increasing demand for rapid and expedient delivery. But to realize the benefits of such technology, there is a need to examine how these technologies affect community well-being and quality of life, as well as to optimize device engineering for accessibility. This grant sought to examine the impacts of new mobility technologies on the communities in which they are deployed, with particular focus on identifying and avoiding potential harms and developing designs the center local community needs. Our goals for this planning grant were as follows: 

  • Generate empirical insights on the factors that promote or hinder the deployment of new mobility technologies, with particular focus on the adaptations required to make PDDs equitable in their local contexts 
  • Co-design failure analysis techniques to inform government decision-making around new mobility 
  • Develop equity metrics to evaluate deployments underway
  • Co-construct a community-centered design and development process for mobility devices 

To achieve these goals, we drew on and extended our existing partnership with the City of Pittsburgh’s Department of Mobility and Infrastructure to form collaborations with a set of diverse participants from across all regions of Pittsburgh, with a particular focus on under-resourced communities, those disconnected from reliable public transit options, residents with disabilities, and older adults. Our community-driven research approach produced a robust understanding of the unintended harms a subset of micromobility devices known as sidewalk robots introduce and, in collaboration with community members, offered a set of potential opportunities to support resident safety and ensure community benefit. Finally, we drew out insights for policymakers and designers from the novel context of publicly deployed robots, which rely on shared, municipal sidewalks to operate. 

 

Intellectual Merit 

The increasing presence of new mobility technologies across municipalities in the United States will have lasting impact on the equity and accessibility of public space, and represents a crucial environment in which to collect data that will inform the future of transit infrastructure. This project produced (1) empirical findings on the factors that promote or hinder the deployment of new mobility technologies, with particular focus on the adaptations required to make PDDs equitable in their local contexts (e.g., device design iteration, oversight), (2) co-designed failure analysis techniques (e.g., games, simulation) to inform government decision-making around new mobility (e.g., procurement and regulation), (3) equity metrics to evaluate deployments underway, and (4) a community-centered design and development process for mobility devices. 

 

Broader Impacts 

Autonomous delivery robots are poised to disproportionately impact elderly residents and those with mobility impairments, who are often not included in their design and deployment. This project produced insights around publicly deployed PPDs, with the intent of enhancing new mobility planning by brokering public conversations around safer community-centered deployments and equitable distribution of benefits. Broader impacts of this research include a workshop series which facilitated community-based discussions and activities. This work also involved translating research insights for consumption by multiple stakeholders—including community groups, industry practitioners, and local government officials—on recognizing the unanticipated consequences of public deployments and enhancing equity.

abstractText:
Image sensors for thermal wavebands of light are usually noisy and subject to nuisance variations. Yet, it is indisputable that thermal imaging has the potential to spur numerous scientific and engineering applications that can fundamentally transform our society. For example, autonomous vehicles equipped with thermal cameras can navigate in the dark and through fog and rain. The widespread availability of thermal imaging technology could usher in methods for non-intrusive vital sign monitoring in public spaces, thereby providing a new tool in our public health arsenal, as well as enable environmental and ecosystem monitoring at both local and global scales. This project seeks to enable such applications with inexpensive but noisy thermal sensors. The research advances made in this progress will be integrated with an educational and outreach program that includes creating new undergraduate and graduate courses, engaging undergraduates in research, and engaging with K-12 communities.

The focus of this research is to advance thermal scene understanding by developing foundational tools for rendering, modeling and imaging at thermal wavebands. The project will develop a physically accurate rendering pipeline for thermal wavebands, that incorporates wavelength-dependent thermal emissivity of complex surfaces, thermal propagation in atmosphere, and accurate sensor modeling and noise characterization. This modeling will be used to design and develop novel computational imaging systems that allow capture of multi-dimensional thermal signals, such as multi-spectral and polarization measurements. The research will also develop a differentiable renderer and exploit it within an end-to-end learning framework for inverse graphics. This will allow for significant improvements in problems such as denoising, super-resolution, stereo, object detection and others. The advances in research will be used to explore and advance autonomous navigation, remote health monitoring and remote environmental monitoring.

projectOutComesReport:
Heat and its transport are omnipresent in the world around us. Whether it be sunlight heating up a large outdoor scene, or a kettle on the stove, or even a person emitting warmth, the effects of conduction, convection and radiation provide a unique window into a scene and its properties. Yet much of this is ignored in traditional computer vision that concentrates solely on imagery in visible spectra of light. In reality, visible light and heat are fundamentally coupled as light that is absorbed heats materials, and as an object heats up it radiates more thermal energy as infrared light. This project looks broadly at heat transport and how leveraging it provides tractable solutions to classical and hard inverse problems in computer vision.

Intellectual Merit. This project aims to advance computational imaging in thermal wavebands, with the eventual goal of advancing scene understanding using thermal cameras. We have developed a detailed theory of visible to thermal light transport, studying how illumination in the visible spectra of light is absorbed, converted to heat, and leads to changes in measurements made by a thermal camera. This has allowed us to develop a suite of technique for solving the so-called intrinsic image decomposition problem, where we estimate the incident illumination energy and the scene’s reflectance property. Our insight here is that looking at the visible and thermal imagery jointly allows us to do an energy budgeting, that in turn allows us to estimate how illumination energy varies spatially, and how objects reflect and absorb it.

Our work in heat transport has also led to new methods for estimating the shape of objects. Our approach uses properties of heat conduction on objects when illuminated using simple light bulbs and shows that a rich description of the shape of the object can be recovered from imaging heat conduction. We have characterized the resulting ambiguities in shape that such method have, providing approaches to mitigate them. Our work has also looked at how visible-to-thermal transport can be used to create ephemeral heat patterns on a scene, which we showed is invaluable for camera motion estimation. Together, these techniques have enabled a richer understanding of thermal imaging and its relationship to visible light, providing new algorithms and tools for scene understanding.

Broader Impacts. The project has achieved educational and scientific impact through multiple channels. Our research has been disseminated through publications at premier computer vision and computational photography conferences. We have also presented posters at workshops and technical events for broader dissemination. Both PIs, Sankaranarayanan and Narasimhan, have given invited talks on the research performed in this project. We have explored the use of these visible-thermal transport to study biological systems like plants to understand the state of the plant in terms of energy budget and the efficiency of the photosynthesis process.

We have organized a course at SIGGRAPH Asia 2025 on “Vision, Imaging, and Simulation for Heat and Light” to publicize and disseminate the research outcomes of this project. The short course exposed participants to the basic theory and practical techniques for heat-light interactions, an understanding of the state-of-the-art, and opening new research directions at the intersection of thermal vision, imaging, and physics-based simulation.

abstractText:
The transition to 5G is expected to witness not only an emergence of new applications such as mobile augmented and virtual reality, but also opens up the attack surface to both known, and previously unknown threats. Thus, wireless networks of the future will need better control and management at different temporal and traffic aggregation granularities (e.g., how to allocate spectrum, how to quarantine distributed attacks etc.).  This project aims to develop scalable, machine learning based analytics on the data from a large set of geographically distributed wireless core network entities such as base stations. The research will enable new approaches for: (a) compressing the raw data via novel summaries and sketches, that reduce overhead while simultaneously enabling highly accurate scalable analytics (b) scalable yet highly flexible distributed learning approaches that are built upon the emerging federated learning paradigm and (c) flexible allocation of bandwidth to support the control plane analytics that minimizes the impact on the data plane. 

The proposed research outcomes will be systems, algorithms, and data analytics workflows that will inform the design and management of next generation critical wireless infrastructures. The approaches developed will enable ISPs to better apportion resources and enable better performance for emerging augmented reality applications for societal benefit (e.g., disaster response and management). In addition, the approaches can enable the discovery and profiling of new threats, which will have significant implications on national security.  The proposed education activities are expected to provide students with a comprehensive training in networking, security, system building, and data science. Thus, there is significant potential for broader impact in terms of contributions to workforce development in an area of national need.

abstractText:
Machine learning algorithms have revolutionized many fields by giving them the ability to use historical data for making predictions or detecting patterns that can then be used to automate various tasks and create new applications for users. The data that many of today’s machine learning applications require, however, is often collected by a network of multiple sensors. For example, data from environmental sensors in smart cities can be used to predict air pollution or traffic at different locations in the city. Analyzing this data with machine learning algorithms then requires these devices to cooperate with each other, exchanging data and models. This project designs mechanisms for devices to efficiently cooperate.

Distributing machine learning algorithms is particularly challenging when devices are heterogeneously resource-constrained, e.g., with varying compute, power, or bandwidth limitations, as is often the case in today’s networks. Traditional learning algorithms either bring all data to a single location for analysis, or entirely distribute the learning algorithm to the data sources. A more flexible approach that instead intelligently brings data to the computing components of the learning algorithms, and conversely brings computing to data sources, can better harness these devices’ resources, but raises a natural question of how data and model components should be moved through the network. This project develops a data-centric approach to distributed learning that utilizes advances in Named Data Networking (NDN) to simplify the process of exchanging information, enabling new types of distributed learning algorithms.

The outcomes of this project may improve the distributed learning in a vast number of potential applications, ranging from smart cities to satellite data analysis to augmented reality. The project also supports ongoing efforts in education and broadening participation in computing to underrepresented communities. These efforts include (i) development of new course materials that teach students about the challenges of realistic machine learning deployments, (ii) recruitment of high school and undergraduate students to work on suitably scoped projects that will contribute to the research vision, and (iii) presentations and mentoring sessions aimed at increasing the participation of underrepresented minorities in computing.

This project is a collaborative effort between Carnegie Mellon University and Northeastern University. Results, including algorithm implementations, technical reports, and measurement datasets, will be made publicly available on a repository hosted by CMU. These will remain available for at least two years after the conclusion of the project.

abstractText:
Driven by its performance accuracy, machine learning (ML) has been used extensively for various applications in the healthcare domain. Despite its promising performance, researchers and the public have grown alarmed by two unsettling deficiencies of these otherwise useful and powerful models. First, there is a lack of trustworthiness - ML models are prone to interference or deception and exhibit erratic behaviors when in action dealing with unseen data, despite good practice during the training phase. Second, there is a lack of interpretability - ML models have been described as 'black-boxes' because there is little explanation for why the models make the predictions they do. This has called into question the applicability of ML to decision-making in critical scenarios such as image-based disease diagnostics or medical treatment recommendation. The ultimate goal of this project is to develop computational foundation for trustworthy and explainable Artificial Intelligence (AI), and offer a low-cost and non-invasive ML-based approach to early diagnosis of neurodegenerative diseases. In particular, the project aims to develop computational theories, ML algorithms, and prototype systems. The project includes developing principled solutions to trustworthy ML and making the ML prediction process transparent to end-users. The later will focus on explaining how and why an ML model makes such a prediction, while dissecting its underlying structure for deeper understanding. The proposed models are further extended to a multi-modal and spatial-temporal framework, an important aspect of applying ML models to healthcare. A verification framework with end-users is defined, which will further enhance the trustworthiness of the prototype systems. This project will benefit a variety of high-impact AI-based applications in terms of their explainability, trustworthy, and verifiability. It not only advances the research fronts of deep learning and AI, but also supports transformations in diagnosing neurodegenerative diseases. 

This project will develop the computational foundation for trustworthy and explainable AI with several innovations. First, the project will systematically study the trustworthiness of ML systems. This will be measured by novel metrics such as, adversarial robustness and semantic saliency, and will be carried out to establish the theoretical basis and practical limits of trustworthiness of ML algorithms. Second, the project provides a paradigm shift for explainable AI, explaining how and why a ML model makes its prediction, moving away from ad-hoc explanations (i.e. what features are important to the prediction). A proof-based approach, which probes all the hidden layers of a given model to identify critical layers and neurons involved in a prediction from a local point of view, will be devised. Third, a verification framework, where users can verify the model's performance and explanations with proofs, will be designed to further enhance the trustworthiness of the system. Finally, the project also advances the frontier of neurodegenerative diseases early diagnosis from multimodal imaging and longitudinal data by: (i) identifying retinal vasculature biomarkers using proof-based probing in biomarker graph networks; (ii) connecting biomarkers of the retina and the brain vasculature via cross- modality explainable AI model; and, (iii) recognizing the longitudinal trajectory of vasculature biomarkers via a spatio-temporal recurrent explainable model. This synergistic effort between computer science and medicine will enable a wide range of applications to trustworthy and explainable AI for healthcare. The results of this project will be assimilated into the courses and summer programs that the research team have developed with specially designed projects to train students with trustworthy and explainable AI.

abstractText:
Group testing is a screening technique that relies on careful combinatorial mixing and testing of batches of samples. By using group testing instead of individual testing, for most problem settings of practical interest, one is guaranteed significant savings in the number of tests performed and consequently, significant reductions in reporting delays and experimental costs. Group testing is especially desirable when monitoring the spread of infectious diseases such as Covid-19, which requires frequent examinations of massive populations. Although many ad-hoc approaches to group testing for infectious diseases have been put forward, little work has addressed the problem of end-to-end group-testing protocol design, which includes the selection of genetic regions for viral/bacterial identification, mathematical modeling and analysis of the test results and the development of guiding protocols for communal testing strategies. The overarching goals of the project are to determine which group-testing methods can actually mitigate the spread of Covid-19 and other diseases and to what extent, to estimate the reduction in the number of infected individuals achievable through the use of pooled real-time polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) tests, and to aid in the employment of Mobile Testing Units that can reach geographically remote regions. Other broader societal impacts include increased readiness for fighting future pandemics and training a new cohort of young researchers on interdisciplinary topics involving machine learning, coding theory and bioinformatics. 

The project aims to develop specialized machine-learning, combinatorial and information-theoretic methods for (a) identifying genomic regions with predictably low-mutation rates that may be used as amplification primers for gold-standard real-time polymerase chain reactions (RT-PCR) and determining best mixing strategies based on the likelihood of infection; (b) developing adequate models for amplification curves generated by RT-PCR and corresponding test-errors; (c) formulating experimental-protocol-specific non-adaptive and adaptive semiquantitative group testing schemes that account for nonbinary test outcomes; (d) addressing the testing issues associated with high-viral load subjects and heavy-hitter communities; and (e) integrating the mathematical techniques developed into an agent-based model for disease spreading and control in order to assess the potential impact of group testing and recommend effective test-quarantine-retest strategies.

abstractText:
With the growth of the Internet and its importance in supporting the US economy, business, health, education and other services, it is critical to ensure both high performance and high availability of the networks underlying it.  Increasingly, such networks include a heterogeneous set of network switches and other devices which must be monitored and controlled in a coordinated manner.  Emerging networked applications, such as cloud gaming or cloud streamed augmented reality, are expected to further stress both control systems and network monitoring by requiring real-time response to rapid changes in traffic workloads. This project aims to address the needs of future network control by enabling a network telemetry infrastructure that can provide timely, accurate, and trusted information about ongoing activities in the network


This project proposes FROOT, a future-proof, trustworthy telemetry infrastructure for networks of heterogeneous programmable devices (e.g., programmable switch, SmartNIC, CPU, and DPU). The project takes an interdisciplinary approach spanning algorithms, systems, and security to inform the design and implementation of next generation telemetry systems through the following: (1) universal sketch-based algorithmic design and implementation for current and new measurement tasks and network devices; (2) novel network-wide resource optimization for handling network dynamics; and (3) trustworthy sketch deployment into heterogeneous devices to obtain critical telemetry information. The researchers also plan to deploy their network telemetry system at Mass Open Cloud testbed, an open public cloud project led by Boston University and other institutions in Massachusetts.  The project will result in the development of open-source tools, algorithms, and prototype implementations that will reduce the time to deploy sketch-based telemetry in real-world scenarios.

projectOutComesReport:
With the growth of the Internet and its importance in supporting the US economy, business, health, education, and other services, it is critical to ensure both high performance and high availability of the networks underlying it. Increasingly, such networks include a heterogeneous set of network devices that must be monitored and controlled in a coordinated manner. Emerging networked applications, such as critical cloud services or cloud-streamed augmented reality, are expected to further stress both control systems and network monitoring by requiring real-time response to rapid changes in network traffic. This project aims to address the needs of future network control by enabling a network telemetry infrastructure that can provide timely, accurate, and trusted information about ongoing activities in the network.

This project challenges the status quo by developing a network-wide telemetry framework for networks that contain the latest innovations in network programmable devices, such as programmable switches, program network interface cards, and data processing units. The Future-pROOf,Trustworthy telemetry (FROOT) system is designed to provide accurate, trustworthy, and real-time measurements for a broad range of current and possibly unforeseen applications across several network domains, including Internet service providers and cloud environments. In particular, realizing the FROOT vision required addressing several research challenges in this project:

  • Telemetry algorithm design and implementation: Telemetry algorithms should be adaptable to unforeseen network issues, such as attacks or performance anomalies. These algorithms need to be efficiently implemented across diverse platforms to enable real-time, accurate measurement. The collaborative research in the project has resulted in efficient and scalable algorithms and their implementations, such as OctoSketch for high-performance monitoring on individual servers and SketchLib for optimized algorithm implementation on network devices.

  • Network-wide resource management: Efficient deployment of telemetry primitives requires intelligent resource allocation to optimize usage and minimize latency. Given the heterogeneity of network hardware architectures, effective placement strategies must balance performance and resilience, ensuring adaptability to device failures and dynamic network conditions. The project developed HeteroSketch, a network-wide telemetry coordination framework that optimally places monitoring tasks across up to 40K heterogeneous devices, balancing efficiency and accuracy.

  • Trustworthy deployment and query: When telemetry capabilities are deployed to the devices in the network, the system must guarantee that the measured results truthfully reflect the underlying network traffic and operators should be able to verify the correctness of the results and use them for their critical services. The project advanced the security of such network telemetry infrastructure with TrustSketch, a trusted execution environment-based system that protects measurement integrity against potential cyberattacks. 

These innovations have been validated and evaluated through peer-reviewed publications and real-world collaborations with industrial partners in the US. Beyond research, the FROOT project has supported education and workforce development efforts by integrating related network research topics into university courses, mentoring undergraduate student projects, and releasing open-source tools for widespread adoption. Our work contributes to autonomous network management, cloud security, and network performance, with future efforts focused on deploying telemetry solutions at scale and collaborating with open-source communities. These contributions ensure that FROOT’s impact continues beyond the NSF funding period, shaping the future of, intelligent, and trustworthy network monitoring. More details are available at the Project Website: https://zaoxing.github.io/projects/frootsecure.

Iowa State University (ISU) in partnership with researchers at the Education Development Center (EDC) and the University of North Carolina Charlotte will implement an NSF EHR Core Research (ECR) project to study the experiences, perspectives, and stories of successful doctoral students and recent PhDs from underrepresented groups in mathematics. The project will develop interview instruments and conduct in-depth, semi-structured interviews with four cohorts: newly accepted students, early graduate students (pre-qualifying exams), advanced graduate students (dissertation level), and recent PhDs (0-5 years since graduation).  The interview instruments could be useful to the field beyond this project and the use of these four cohorts will add to the current literature.  The research questions in the study are: What are lived experiences of successful underrepresented students who are pursuing mathematics PhDs? and What formal and informal structures are perceived by doctoral students as effective supports? 

The research will build knowledge to inform decisions about changing mathematics department cultures and practices to better recruit, retain and graduate mathematicians from underrepresented groups.  The project will result in survey results from 100 graduate students and recent graduates and twelve composite counterstories illustrating the student experiences and support systems that result in success for students from underrepresented groups.  The counterstories and other results are expected to disrupt current perceptions about who can be successful in graduate school, and how.   The project includes plans for strategic dissemination of the research results to stakeholders and practitioners.

projectOutComesReport:
Studying Successful Doctoral Students in Mathematics from Underrepresented Groups, a project, led by Michael Young and co-investigators Sarah Sword and Carl Westine, examines the experiences of successful doctoral students from underrepresented groups in mathematics. The study addresses critical challenges faced by minoritized students pursuing mathematics PhDs, aiming to understand systemic structures that support their success. The team conducted in-depth, semi-structured interviews with 75 participants, including doctoral students and recent PhDs, to identify effective mentoring practices, social and financial supports, and barriers to success.

Key Research Questions
The study explores two primary questions:

  1. What are the lived experiences of successful underrepresented students pursuing mathematics PhDs?
  2. What formal and informal structures are effective in supporting their success?

Emerging Themes
The data revealed several recurring themes:

  • Isolation and Invisibility: Many students reported feelings of isolation due to being the only minoritized individuals in their departments or being treated as invisible. These experiences varied but often included lack of cultural understanding, microaggressions, and being held to higher standards than peers.
  • Social Capital: Successful students relied heavily on networks for guidance and support. Relationships within their departments, broader academic communities, and among mathematicians of color were critical. Communication breakdowns and lack of access to informal knowledge about navigating graduate school were identified as barriers.
  • Financial Challenges: Students without financial safety nets faced significant stress navigating stipends, salaries, and the timing of payments. Practical financial support was often critical for their success.
  • Mentorship: Effective mentoring emerged as a pivotal factor. Ideal mentors were described as empathetic, proactive, and trustworthy, offering personalized guidance, making hidden pathways visible, and advocating for their mentees.

Outcomes and Implications
The study provides actionable insights for improving recruitment, retention, and success of underrepresented groups in mathematics PhDs. Key recommendations include:

  1. Fostering open, one-on-one communication with students to understand their individual needs.
  2. Encouraging faculty to adopt collaborative approaches in mentoring and supporting students.
  3. Creating opportunities for students to share their experiences, both informally and through institutional channels.

The findings highlight the importance of addressing systemic inequities, improving cultural competence in departments, and establishing robust mentoring networks. By understanding the lived experiences of successful students, mathematics departments can implement targeted strategies to create more inclusive and supportive environments.

The project underscores the value of listening to students' voices and tailoring interventions to their specific needs, paving the way for meaningful and lasting change in the field of mathematics education.

abstractText:
Advances in natural language processing (NLP) technology now make it possible to perform many tasks through natural language or over natural language data -- automatic systems can answer questions, perform web search, or command our computers to perform specific tasks. However, ``language'' is not monolithic; people vary in the language they speak, the dialect they use, the relative ease with which they produce language, or the words they choose with which to express themselves. In benchmarking of NLP systems however, this linguistic variety is generally unattested. Most commonly tasks are formulated using canonical American English, designed with little regard for whether systems will work on language of any other variety. In this work we ask a simple question: can we measure the extent to which the diversity of language that we use affects the quality of results that we can expect from language technology systems? This will allow for the development and deployment of fair accuracy measures for a variety of tasks regarding language technology, encouraging advances in the state of the art in these technologies to focus on all, not just a select few.

Specifically, this work focuses on four aspects of this overall research question. First, we will develop a general-purpose methodology for quantifying how well particular language technologies work across many varieties of language. Measures over multiple speakers or demographics are combined to benchmarks that can drive progress in development of fair metrics for language systems, tailored to the specific needs of design teams. Second, we will move beyond simple accuracy measures, and directly quantify the effect that the accuracy of systems has on users in terms of relative utility derived from using the system. These measures of utility will be incorporated in our metrics for system success. Third, we focus on the language produced by people from varying demographic groups, predicting system accuracies from demographics. Finally, we will examine novel methods for robust learning of NLP systems across language or dialectal boundaries, and examine the effect that these methods have on increasing accuracy for all users.

projectOutComesReport:
Advances in natural language processing (NLP) technology now make it possible to perform many tasks through natural language or over natural language data -- automatic systems can answer questions, perform web search, or command our computers to perform specific tasks. However, ``language'' is not monolithic; people vary in the language they speak, the dialect they use, the relative ease with which they produce language, or the words they choose with which to express themselves. In benchmarking of NLP systems however, this linguistic variety is generally unattested. Most commonly tasks are formulated using canonical American English, designed with little regard for whether systems will work on language of any other variety. In this work we asked a simple question: can we measure the extent to which the diversity of language that we use affects the quality of results that we can expect from language technology systems? This will allow for the development and deployment of fair accuracy measures for a variety of tasks regarding language technology, encouraging advances in the state of the art in these technologies to focus on all, not just a select few.


Specifically, this work focused on several aspects of this overall research question:

  • First, the project developed a general-purpose methodology for quantifying how well particular language technologies work across many varieties of language. It built benchmarks that considered the overall speaking population for various language varieties and built a benchmark GlobalBench.
  • Second, it moved beyond simple accuracy measures, and directly quantified the effect that the accuracy of systems has on users in terms of relative utility derived from using the system. For instance, it examined the disparate effect of mistakes in voice recognition on people of various demographics.
  • Third, it examined novel methods for robust learning of NLP systems across language or dialectal boundaries, and examine the effect that these methods have on increasing accuracy for all users. For instance, it created techniques that can generate text in many different language varieties.

title: FAI: Quantifying and Mitigating Disparities in Language Technologies

abstractText:
Government agencies and the public sector have increasingly turned to data-driven and Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based techniques to enhance the quality of human decision-making and service provision. This shift toward an AI-driven approach holds promise in its ability to offer much-needed support to understaffed departments and increasing the speed with which community members’ concerns are met. However, an over-emphasis on efficiency and effectiveness, along with most AI-based systems’ lack of transparency into how a given recommendation is made, have made it difficult for public sector workers to make fair, equitable, efficient decisions. This can result in lack of accountability to constituents and cause harm to minoritized communities, as demonstrated by cases such as racial bias in predictive policing systems. This project will use a service design-inspired approach to investigate how public sector data and algorithmic infrastructures are formed, factors that can lead to disparate municipal service provision, and how these infrastructures might be redesigned to address the inequities they sometimes reinforce. This planning grant will give the project team additional insight into the problem while helping the team build community partnerships and expand its disciplinary expertise, in order to develop a larger, long-term research agenda. 

The project involves four major activities, which will be conducted in the context of business owners’ interaction with public sector permit, license, and inspection departments that use or plan to use data-innovation and AI-enhanced decision-making tools. The first activity involves characterizing the current state of data collected and analyzed using a data audit methodology, with the goal of identifying needed changes to disaggregate business owners by qualities related to equity and fairness and to support business process mining. The second and third activities are to understand the priorities and experiences of public sector workers who make decisions about permits, licenses, and inspections, and the experience and challenges faced by local, small, women- and minority-owned businesses that need these services in order to launch their ventures. Those activities will be based on interviews with members of the respective populations, culminating in a fourth activity in which these stakeholder groups will come together with the research team in co-design workshops to help define and balance the key objectives held by all stakeholders, along with ideas for how systems can be shaped to achieve those objectives in AI-based systems that support public sector decision making.

projectOutComesReport:
This research project, conducted in partnership with the City of Pittsburgh’s Office of Permits, Licenses, and Inspections (PLI), aims to evaluate and improve equity in public service work, with a focus on urban development and the impact on businesses, particularly minority-owned ones. Key aspects of the project include:

  • Objective: The project seeks to understand current inequitable practices in public sector work, investigate the effects of public sector technology on equity, envision alternative, more equitable futures for public technology, and comprehend the complexities of integrating equity in technology design.

  • Activities: The research involved interviewing diverse stakeholders, including city staff and local business owners, to assess the impact of digital systems and political goals like supporting local businesses. It also included future-looking interviews with local business owners, particularly minority- and women-owned businesses, to discuss equitable public sector visions. This project also involved a systematic literature review on the challenges of embedding equity in technology.

  • Findings:

    • The transition to an online system was found to exacerbate inequities, particularly affecting first-time business owners through reduced face-to-face interactions, increased fear of bias, and systemic challenges in the building department. There was a misalignment between departmental standardization priorities and community equity values.

    • The research revealed that monitoring equity could paradoxically intensify disparities. However, demographic-based analysis was seen as valuable for identifying discrimination and supporting minority businesses. Participants favored a holistic approach to equity, emphasizing community needs over identity-based advantages, and expressed concerns about the reliability of public sector information.

    • The literature review on integrating equity in technology design highlighted the difficulties in defining and operationalizing equity in technology, describing it as a “wicked” problem with various tensions and trade-offs.

  • Implications and Future Work: The project underscores the complexities and challenges of achieving equitable public service delivery in the context of digital transformation, highlighting the need for thoughtful integration of equity in technology design and public sector practices.

abstractText:
Voice based interactions have become the norm everywhere from cars, to mobile phones to digital home assistants. As speech based machine interaction becomes more pervasive, there is increased demand and expectation of human-like performance and personality from these systems. It is important for the machine to deliver responses about the weather on a pleasant sunny day or an impending hurricane in an appropriate manner. Machines need to be able to respond sympathetically or emphatically depending on the context of their use. Critically, when machines fail, they should do so in human understandable ways, so that there are no unintended consequences of technology. This project aims to create more natural and flexible speech synthesis technology that is inspired by human strategies and mechanisms for speech production. Bringing together the science of speech production and current state-of-the-art engineering speech systems, this project aims to impart explainability, naturalness and flexibility to speech technologies. This project has the potential to impact all systems that use speech output like automated tutoring, interactive voice response, speech translation in commercial and military settings, digital assistants, robotics and rehabilitative healthcare applications like Brain-Computer Interfaces. 

Current speech synthesis techniques are focused on end-to-end systems, avoiding explicit modeling of internal structure of the speech signal. Consequently, such systems may have good results but fail to allow any generalization beyond their recorded databases. This project concentrates on incorporating aspects of human speech production into computer speech synthesis. Using data-driven techniques and vocal tract imaging datasets, the project aims to discover and model compositional aspects of the speech signal as described by Articulatory Phonology. Novel deep-learning based approaches will be developed for joint optimization of diverse speech representations such as acoustic, phonological and physiological data within an analysis-by-synthesis framework. New strategies will be developed for incorporating grounded representations into text-to-speech training and evaluated in a range of applications in flexible speech synthesis.

projectOutComesReport:
This project has made significant contributions to advancing speech synthesis, particularly in integrating gestural modeling within sequence-to-sequence text-to-speech (TTS) systems. Over the course of the past three years, our work has focused on deep neural network techniques, unsupervised gesture discovery, and the development of open-source frameworks that push the boundaries of TTS performance and evaluation.

2022 Outcomes: Establishing the Foundation for Gestural Modeling in TTS

In 2022, our primary focus was on laying the groundwork for integrating gestural modeling into sequence-to-sequence TTS systems. Our team at Carnegie Mellon University (CMU) conducted a series of experiments and launched regular bi-weekly meetings with core team members to streamline the process. One of our key achievements was the development of an experimental pipeline for sequence-to-sequence deep speech synthesis methods. We focused on three critical aspects:

  1. Data Preparation: We established methods for preparing articulatory representations and corresponding waveforms, which are crucial for accurate gestural modeling.

  2. Exploring Neural Architectures: After experimenting with various architectures, we found that the HiFiGAN-based neural vocoder provided promising results for our problem, offering high-quality speech synthesis with enhanced naturalness and intelligibility.

  3. Evaluation Metrics: We established robust evaluation metrics and analysis methods to ensure the validity and reliability of our synthesized speech outputs.

These outcomes were published at Interspeech 2022, contributing to the broader understanding of TTS systems and their capabilities.

2023 Outcomes: Expanding Neural Architectures and Unsupervised Gesture Discovery

Building on the progress of 2022, in 2023, we expanded our efforts to incorporate unsupervised gesture discovery using Non-negative Matrix Factorization (NMF) and further enhanced the neural architectures within our TTS systems. Our team continued regular bi-weekly meetings and applied the experimental pipeline to devise new, state-of-the-art TTS methods. Notable advancements include:

  1. New Neural Architectures: We integrated state-of-the-art self-supervised learning (SSL) models to improve the robustness and generalization of our speech synthesis methods, achieving superior performance in a variety of speech contexts.

  2. Application to Other Sensor Data: We extended our methodology beyond speech by applying it to other sensor data, such as MRI data, demonstrating the versatility and potential of our framework in multimodal data analysis.

Our findings were shared in leading speech conferences, such as ICASSP'23 and Interspeech'23, reinforcing our contribution to advancing TTS research and development.

2024 Outcomes: Open-Source Framework and Evaluation Toolkit

In 2024, we made significant strides in creating tools that would enable the broader research community to reproduce and build upon our work. A major outcome was the development of an open-source framework under the ESPnet project, which allowed for the reproduction of five major neural audio codecs, including Encodec and DAC that models that had not been open-sourced before. These codecs are integral to building high-performance sequence-to-sequence TTS systems integrated with gestural modeling.

To support fair comparisons and high-performance evaluations, we also developed the VERSA toolkit (https://github.com/shinjiwlab/versa). This toolkit is dedicated to collecting over 50 evaluation metrics for synthesized speech, addressing various aspects such as clarity, intelligibility, speaker similarity, signal-level distortion, emotion, and semantic information. VERSA facilitates the following:

  1. High-Performance Speech Synthesis: The toolkit enables the production of very high-quality synthesized speech based on neural codecs, empowering researchers to achieve cutting-edge results.

  2. Fair Comparisons Across Codecs: We designed the framework to allow easy manipulation of training data, model architecture, and configurations, ensuring reproducibility and fair comparisons across different codecs.

  3. Comprehensive Evaluation: Recognizing the difficulty of evaluating synthesized speech, VERSA provides a comprehensive set of metrics to evaluate multiple facets of speech generation, ensuring a holistic approach to quality assessment.

These outcomes were presented at IEEE SLT 2024, further advancing the field of speech synthesis and providing tools for the broader community to push the boundaries of neural codec-based TTS systems.

Intellectual Merit and Broader Impacts

The intellectual merit of this project lies in its significant contributions to the development of advanced neural architectures, the integration of gestural modeling in TTS, and the establishment of open-source tools that promote transparency and reproducibility in speech synthesis research. Our work pushes the boundaries of TTS by incorporating unsupervised gesture discovery and self-supervised learning, enhancing the robustness and naturalness of synthesized speech.

The broader impacts of our work are multifaceted. By providing open-source code, model weights, and the VERSA evaluation toolkit, we are empowering the research community to replicate and extend our findings. Our work also has the potential to impact real-world applications in conversational AI, speech therapy, and multimodal data analysis, contributing to advancements in both speech technology and interdisciplinary research.

abstractText:
IoT devices such as smart door locks and platforms and applications that connect these devices and other online services (e.g., IFTTT, Zapier) make life more convenient but have also raised security and privacy concerns. These concerns arise because smart home devices can collect potentially sensitive data about their users and the data and devices can be accessed (e.g., to unlock doors or disable home security systems) in the absence of physical human actions. Further, the risks posed by smart-home devices can impact people other than the device owners, such as home service workers and children. There is a need for a systematic understanding of the security and privacy impact of such platforms. However, existing work is often too coarse-grained to capture the context in which these devices are used (e.g., camera in public area vs. in the bedroom) and mostly focuses on risks and harms to device owners rather than more broadly. This project aims to gain a deeper understanding of smart homes' security and privacy impact, with a focus on end-user programming platforms like IFTTT and Zapier, and to mitigate potential harms via formal modeling and automated analysis tools.  One of the identifying characteristics of this project is that user studies are used to both identify user needs and to evaluate potential solutions, including models and formal analysis tools.

This project follows an iterative process, where tools and models are first built (based on results of preliminary user studies); next, user studies are conducted to evaluate the tools and learn about users' needs; then, results from user studies are used to refine the tools and models. This project builds detailed, context-rich models and characterizations of risks and harms from home automation platforms, customized to individual users' perspective, and thus fills the gap between what existing models and tools can do and users' perceptions and needs. This project also builds usable, context-aware, configurable analysis tools that extend traditional information-flow analysis to calculate attackers’ precise knowledge of and influence over the system. These analysis tools take into consideration different threat models, which account for attackers’ different capabilities to observe relevant events and interact with the system. Finally, the project designs warnings and nudges to help users understand their smart home systems better and avoid potential harm.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.
